Headline: Experian now runs a separate credit bureau built on bank-account cash flow.
Context: On October 6, 2026 Experian announced Experian Cashflow Data Bureau, Inc., a US consumer reporting agency that turns bank-account transaction and balance data shared by consumers into a report for lenders, though the release names no lender customers.

Headline: Plaid's new cash-flow credit scores let borrowers share bank data once and reuse it on later applications.
Context: In its own launch announcement on October 6, 2026, Plaid (US) introduced LendScore 2, a family of cash-flow risk scores with versions for auto, home and short-term lending, and Instant Link, which spares borrowers from reconnecting a bank account on later credit applications.

Headline: A federal rulebook for getting paid before payday cleared a House committee on a split vote.
Context: The US House Financial Services Committee said on July 1, 2026 that it passed H.R. 9330, the Earned Wage Access Consumer Protection Act, by 29 to 22, a bill that would set a federal regulatory framework for earned wage access services.

Headline: The FTC accepts that credit is priced to the individual but wants personalized prices elsewhere disclosed.
Context: In a proposed enforcement policy statement dated August 19, 2026, the US Federal Trade Commission said credit and insurance prices necessarily turn on individual characteristics, while firms that personalize prices where consumers do not expect it should clearly disclose the basis and the types of data used.

Headline: New York lawmakers voted to ban pricing based on personal data but exempted credit priced on creditworthiness.
Context: New York's Assembly and Senate passed bill A9349-B on June 4, 2026, barring surveillance pricing while exempting insurers and prices or terms based on an evaluation of creditworthiness, and the legislature's bill page showed no action by the governor when checked on November 19, 2026.

Headline: Most Americans are uneasy about letting an AI agent move their money.
Context: A Morning Consult poll of 4,402 US adults for the American Bankers Association, fielded October 9-12, 2026, found 77% are concerned about giving an AI tool or agent permission to move money or make payments, and only 27% say they are likely to let an AI agent manage their bank cash balances on its own in the next 12 months.

Headline: Interest in letting AI directly manage money is low and has fallen over the past year.
Context: PYMNTS Intelligence's US consumer surveys found 16% of respondents in July-September 2026 were interested in giving AI authority to manage their money directly, down from 20% in September-November 2025.

Headline: People will let AI protect their money or pay a bill they already approved, but most are not ready to hand over day-to-day money management.
Context: An FIS-sponsored online survey of 2,000 US adults, fielded September 16-30, 2026 with a Kantar sample, found 57% comfortable with AI freezing a suspicious charge without asking and 55% with it paying a previously approved recurring bill, while 37% said they were ready to hand day-to-day money management to an AI assistant and 49% said they were not.

Headline: Most Americans would let their bank's AI assistant handle at least one financial task for them.
Context: A TD Bank survey of 1,008 US respondents, run by Big Village on September 18-20, 2026, found 69% would allow a bank-provided AI assistant to complete at least one financial task on their behalf, though 36% named human review of important decisions as a key safeguard.

Headline: Robinhood now lets customers' AI agents place stock trades, but only from a separate account with its own balance.
Context: As reported on May 27, 2026, Robinhood's agentic trading launched in beta and is limited to stocks: users load a dedicated account for the agent, the agent cannot reach their full brokerage balance, and users are notified of every trade.

Headline: The US rule giving consumers a right to share their bank data is being rewritten and has been waiting on White House review since August.
Context: US: the CFPB's proposed rule, titled Personal Financial Data Rights Reconsideration, was received for regulatory review on 4 August 2026 and is still listed as pending on the federal review tracker, flagged as economically significant.

Headline: The EU plans to scrap its proposed law that would have extended data sharing from bank accounts to the rest of a customer's finances.
Context: EU: the European Commission's 2027 work programme, dated 4 November 2026, lists the 2023 Financial Data Access proposal among files it intends to withdraw within six months, saying there have been no negotiations since June 2025 and it is unlikely to win Council support.

Headline: Nearly one in three UK adults now uses open banking, and the regulator is moving to extend it to the rest of people's finances.
Context: UK: the Financial Conduct Authority said on 14 April 2026 that open banking has approximately 17 million users and that it will work with HM Treasury on options for an open finance regulatory framework by the end of 2027.

Headline: UK open banking has passed one billion payments and 100 billion data requests, and monthly traffic is still setting records.
Context: UK: Open Banking Limited, the body that runs the system, reported on 30 July 2026 that the nine largest banks had passed both milestones since launch and that June 2026 set a monthly record of 2.81 billion API calls alongside 40.16 million payments.

Headline: Most Americans say they already keep most or all of their finances at one institution, which narrows the audience for a cross-bank view.
Context: US: in a survey of 1,000 consumers fielded via Dynata in Q2 2026 and published by SavvyMoney, a vendor to financial institutions, 42% said they use the same institution for everything and 41% use one for most needs, while 17% spread their finances across several.

Headline: Pay-later credit at checkout has become a market of more than $150 billion a year in the US.
Context: Federal Reserve Board staff estimated in a June 5, 2026 note that six large providers (Affirm, Afterpay, Klarna, PayPal, Sezzle and Zip) issued $156.7 billion of buy now, pay later credit in 2025, with pay-in-4 plans making up 50 percent and about 63 percent carrying 0 percent APR.

Headline: Affirm's pay-over-time volume keeps growing by a third a year, and its card is the fastest-growing part.
Context: Affirm reported in its November 5, 2026 shareholder letter that volume rose 34 percent to $14.4 billion in the quarter ended September 30, 2026, its twelfth straight quarter above 30 percent growth, with Affirm Card volume up 117 percent to $3.3 billion (company-reported figures).

Headline: Pay-later growth is concentrated among cash-strapped shoppers, and it is costing some of them bank fees.
Context: A Federal Reserve publication from August 2026, based on its nationally representative 2025 US household survey of nearly 13,000 respondents, found 16 percent of adults used buy now, pay later in 2025 and 11 percent of users had a payment trigger an overdraft or insufficient-funds fee in the prior year.

Headline: Most Americans are not yet willing to let an AI assistant pay for them.
Context: A Harris Poll survey of 2,065 US consumers sponsored by Visa, fielded May 26-28, 2026 and released September 9, 2026, found only 23 percent trust generative AI to handle payment transactions on their behalf, even though 72 percent have used an AI assistant.

Headline: Google is building checkout directly into Search and its Gemini assistant.
Context: Google announced on May 19, 2026 that a shared shopping cart would roll out across Search and the Gemini app in the US that summer with Google Pay checkout, naming Nike, Sephora, Target, Ulta Beauty, Walmart and Wayfair among merchants due to get checkout features, which shows the launch but not customer uptake.

Headline: Personalization lifts bank customer satisfaction sharply, but few customers say they always get it.
Context: J.D. Power's 2026 U.S. Financial Health Support and Advice Study, released May 27, 2026, found just 20% of US bank customers say their bank always personalizes the information they receive, and satisfaction scores rise 238 points among bank customers when providers get personalization right.

Headline: Most US bank customers feel their bank is not tailoring to them, yet few banks rank personalization as a top priority.
Context: A Celent report commissioned by Temenos and dated August 25, 2026, based on a survey of 2,500 US consumers, found more than half feel their bank is not tailoring products and services well enough, while fewer than 10% of US banks call personalization a top-three priority for 2026.

Headline: Customers draw a line at personalization when AI makes the decision with no human check.
Context: Datos Insights reported on September 3, 2026 that nearly 45% of consumers in its 2026 study of 3,500 US consumers say personalized experiences become unacceptable when AI makes decisions without human review.

Headline: Product recommendations are landing better at national and online-only banks than at regional and community institutions.
Context: A survey of 1,500 American digital banking users, fielded March 26 to April 22, 2026 by The Center for Generational Kinetics for sponsor Alkami, found only 38% of regional and community institution customers say product recommendations have become more relevant, versus 51% at online-only providers and 50% at major national institutions.

Headline: Fewer than three in ten bank and card app customers use the built-in virtual assistant, and it falters on fraud and disputes.
Context: J.D. Power's 2026 U.S. banking and credit card app studies, released in late May 2026, found 28% of national bank and credit card app customers use virtual assistants, and that satisfaction with them drops sharply when customers try to resolve problems, dispute charges or identify fraud.

Headline: Nearly nine in ten customers say a route to a human agent is essential when a company uses AI for service.
Context: A Gartner survey of 3,566 business and consumer customers, fielded in February and March 2026 and published in August 2026, found 87% call a human option essential even though 50% say generative AI makes their interactions easier.

Headline: California has made reaching a human in customer service a legal duty for large businesses.
Context: The California Governor's office announced on September 28, 2026 that AB 1609 was signed, requiring large businesses to make a good-faith effort to connect a customer to a human within 15 minutes of a request or to schedule an appointment.

Headline: New York City has proposed a rule that would require an easy route from an automated service system to a human.
Context: The city's Department of Consumer and Worker Protection published the proposed rule on October 20, 2026 with a 30-day comment period, and if adopted it would make businesses disclose automated customer service and offer an easy way to reach a human representative, with fines starting at $525.

Headline: Few companies have actually cut service staff because of AI, and some are already hiring people back.
Context: In a Gartner survey of 275 service and support leaders fielded in July and August 2026, only 21% said they had reduced human agent headcount because of AI and 7% said they had rehired after earlier cuts, and Gartner predicts half of companies that cut will rehire by 2027.

Pillar: Proactively Protect Customers Against Emerging Threats
Headline: Americans reported a record amount lost to fraud in 2025, and the costliest scams often start with a fake bank security alert.
Context: The US Federal Trade Commission said on June 15, 2026 that about $16 billion was reported lost to fraud in 2025, roughly 25% more than in 2024, including $3.5 billion lost to imposter scams.

Pillar: Proactively Protect Customers Against Emerging Threats
Headline: Once scam money has left the account, even the FBI's rapid freeze process stops only a little over half of it.
Context: The FBI's Internet Crime Report covering 2025 shows its recovery team handled 3,900 incidents with about $1.16 billion in attempted theft and froze about $679 million, a 58% success rate.

Pillar: Proactively Protect Customers Against Emerging Threats
Headline: US banks have no general federal rule for pausing a suspicious electronic payment like the one that lets them hold a suspect check.
Context: A Congressional Research Service note dated November 2, 2026 says the federal fraud exception for holding checks generally has no equivalent for electronic transfers, and that roughly half of states have hold laws that apply to banks.

Pillar: Proactively Protect Customers Against Emerging Threats
Headline: Big US banks are blocking outside AI agents that customers have handed their banking passwords to.
Context: TechTarget reported on November 9, 2026, citing an October Axios report, that Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan Chase and other banks have moved to keep unvetted third-party agents off their platforms, and that banks have no reliable way to tell whether an agent is acting as the customer intended.

Pillar: Proactively Protect Customers Against Emerging Threats
Headline: Shared standards for how customers safely hand tasks to AI agents are only now being written.
Context: The FIDO Alliance said on April 28, 2026 that it has started working groups on agent authentication and agent payments, chaired by members from CVS Health, Google, OpenAI, Mastercard and Visa, and that the specifications are still in development (global).

Headline: FedNow is growing fast, with payment volume up 27.6% in a single quarter.
Context: Federal Reserve data show FedNow settled 6.38 million payments worth about $371 billion in July-September 2026 (US), up from 5.0 million payments and about $275 billion the quarter before.

Headline: Same-day bank transfers are growing far faster than the US ACH network as a whole.
Context: Nacha reported 470.4 million Same Day ACH payments worth $1.3 trillion in the third quarter of 2026 (US), up 36.7% from a year earlier, while total ACH payments rose 5.9% to 9.3 billion.

Headline: Only about one in five US banks and credit unions has joined FedNow, and apps that already feel instant ease the pressure to join.
Context: A Richmond Fed economic brief from August 2026 counts 1,725 FedNow participants, 19.7% of US financial institutions as of the first quarter of 2026, and describes adoption as early and cautious.

Headline: Everyday cross-border payments have become slower, not faster, since 2023.
Context: The Financial Stability Board's November 2026 global progress report found the share of retail cross-border services settling within one hour fell 1.3 percentage points and within one day 14.2 points since 2023, with no measurable progress on average retail cost.

Headline: In the euro area, instant transfers are still a minority of bank transfers, especially by value.
Context: European Central Bank statistics published in July 2026 show instant credit transfers made up 25% of the number and 8% of the value of credit transfers processed by euro area retail payment systems in the second half of 2025.
